questions.prompt: Which instructional design models and learning theories do you actually use in your work?
questions.answer: I know the frameworks, but I do not treat them like a checklist I have to perform for every project. ADDIE is useful when I need a clear end-to-end structure. SAM is helpful when the work needs fast prototypes and repeated review. Backward design is probably the habit I use most consistently because I start with what the learner needs to do, then work backward into objectives, practice, assessment, and content. Bloom helps me keep objectives measurable. Gagne, adult learning principles, and Kirkpatrick are useful lenses when I am thinking about engagement, relevance, transfer, and what evidence is realistic to collect. I use the theory to make better decisions, not to make the project sound academic.

questions.prompt: How do you diagnose whether a performance problem actually needs training?
questions.answer: I start by asking what is happening now, what should be happening instead, and what is actually stopping the person from doing it. If the gap is knowledge, confidence, or practice, training may be the right answer. If the issue is a broken process, bad access, missing documentation, unclear ownership, system friction, or an incentive problem, I would rather fix that than build a course nobody needed. I use an HPI mindset because I want to solve the performance problem, not win an argument for more training. I am also continuing to build formal depth in HPI and related certifications because that consulting side of the work is where I want to keep growing.

questions.prompt: How do you turn a large amount of source material into a coherent curriculum?
questions.answer: I usually start by getting the source material out of document order and into learner-decision order. I map the audience, business need, objectives, dependencies, practice, assessment, and any optional or regional content before I worry about screens. Then I look for what has to come first, what can be referenced later, what is duplicated, and what should not be in the learning at all. For large technical programs, I also separate stable foundations from fast-changing product detail so the curriculum is easier to maintain. That is how I keep a big content set from turning into one giant linear information dump.

questions.prompt: How deep is your accessibility experience beyond adding alt text and captions?
questions.answer: I think about accessibility as part of the interaction design, not a cleanup pass. That means keyboard navigation, logical focus order, semantic structure, readable contrast, captions and transcripts, reduced-motion behavior, clear labels, predictable navigation, and not making meaning depend on color or hover alone. In custom HTML and JavaScript work, I can control those mechanics directly. In authoring tools, I work inside the platform's accessibility model and test the experience instead of assuming a checkbox makes it compliant. I understand the engineering required for strict WCAG 2.2 and Section 508 expectations, and I design toward universal access from the beginning.

questions.prompt: How do you think about xAPI, cmi5, and learning data beyond SCORM completion tracking?
questions.answer: SCORM is fine when all you need is launch, completion, score, and pass or fail. I am interested in the data that explains what happened inside the experience. With xAPI and cmi5, I can think in terms of meaningful events: which decision a learner made, what evidence they selected, where they changed an answer, what path they took, or whether they used a resource before succeeding. I can write custom JavaScript triggers to send those statements and design the statement structure so an LRS, data lake, or BI layer can actually use it. The important part is not tracking everything because you can. It is defining the events that answer a real learning or business question.

questions.prompt: How comfortable are you with the technical ecosystem around an enterprise LMS?
questions.answer: My direct integration work is with LMS exports, account matching, migration crosswalks, and learner-path validation. I map what each system sends or expects, identify who owns the rule, and test exceptions before a learner or completion record is trusted. I also understand how identity, CRM or HR data, content tracking, and reporting fit around the LMS, but the System Integrations page labels those broader examples as platform-informed patterns. I work with identity and backend owners on implementation rather than claiming those roles as mine.

questions.prompt: What does advanced AI use look like in your instructional design work?
questions.answer: For me, advanced AI use is not asking a chatbot to write a course and pasting the result. I am much more interested in structured systems: clear agent instructions, reusable prompt patterns, source boundaries, evaluation rubrics, modular generation, human review, and workflows that move content from one stage to the next without losing context. I have built and tested custom-agent style workflows, used AI for evaluation work, and designed processes where the model has a defined job instead of unlimited creative freedom. I also care a lot about privacy and source control, especially when the content is internal or technical. The goal is to make the ID faster and more consistent without outsourcing judgment.

questions.prompt: How do you apply UX and UI thinking to learning experiences?
questions.answer: I think a learning interface should make the next useful action obvious. I pay attention to hierarchy, navigation, chunking, visual rhythm, interaction cost, responsive behavior, accessibility, and how much the learner has to remember just to use the course. I prototype when the interface itself is part of the problem, and I am comfortable moving between Figma or Adobe XD-style planning, authoring tools, and HTML/CSS/JavaScript when I need more control. Good learning UX is not decoration. It is removing friction so the learner can spend attention on the decision or skill instead of figuring out the interface.

questions.prompt: How do you manage a complex learning project with multiple reviewers, assets, and deadlines?
questions.answer: I make the work visible. I break the project into decisions, dependencies, assets, review points, and launch requirements instead of treating 'build the course' like one task. I use tools such as Asana, Smartsheet, Jira, Monday, Trello, Teams, Slack, and Review 360 depending on the environment, but the tool matters less than having clear owners and a clean approval path. I also separate content review from design review when I can, because mixing every kind of feedback into one giant comment cycle is how projects get slow and weird.

questions.prompt: How do you storyboard or script learning when other people may need to build or review it?
questions.answer: I storyboard to remove ambiguity, not to create another document nobody wants to maintain. I include the learning purpose, screen or interaction intent, copy, visual direction, narration or audio notes when needed, feedback logic, accessibility notes, and anything the developer or reviewer needs to understand the behavior. If I am building the content myself, I can work lighter and prototype sooner. If the work is handed to another developer, designer, or voice talent, I make the specifications much more explicit so the handoff does not depend on reading my mind.
